# Changed O2 Sensor and My Mileage Went Down

It is counterintuitive to replace a component with significant wear, expecting degradation rather than restoration. In your specific case with the 1997 Mazda 323 BA (Lantis), you replaced an original oxygen sensor with approximately 200,000 kilometers on it with a fresh NGK unit sourced from the dealership. Theoretically, this should have improved fuel economy by restoring proper air-fuel ratio feedback to the ECU. Instead, your mileage dropped from roughly 8.3 k/l to 7.9 k/l over 247 kilometers of driving under identical conditions.

The most common reaction is to suspect a calibration mismatch between the new sensor and the Engine Control Unit (ECU). Many modern ECUs utilize "fuel trim" logic where they learn the behavior of aging sensors and compensate accordingly. When you swap a slow-responding, drifted original unit for a fast, precise new one, the ECU may initially interpret the richer or leaner readings as an engine misfire or vacuum leak until it relearns the baseline.

However, there is a critical distinction between learning curves and immediate operational faults. You mentioned resetting the ECU, which on many OBD-II compliant vehicles involves disconnecting the negative battery terminal for 15 to 30 minutes to clear volatile memory and fuel trim adaptations. Since you performed this reset and the mileage remained consistently worse, the issue likely lies in how the new sensor interacts with the existing drivetrain components rather than a simple software mismatch.

The source material notes that turbocharged models require disconnecting the battery before installation, citing an AutoZone guide. While your 1997 Lantis is naturally aspirated, the mechanical procedure for installing O2 sensors often involves heating elements and specific wiring harness connections. If the new sensor has a different resistance curve or heater voltage requirement than the legacy unit the ECU was calibrated against, it could cause the system to run rich as a fail-safe mode, increasing fuel consumption immediately upon start-up until the ECU completes its adaptation cycle post-reset.

Another hidden variable in your diagnostic process is the missing thermostat. You discovered you were driving without one and installed a replacement, yet your MPG did not improve. This suggests that the lack of a thermostat was causing the engine to run cool for extended periods (open loop condition), which inherently lowers fuel efficiency due to unburned hydrocarbons in the exhaust. However, if the ECU has already learned an aggressive enrichment strategy based on the faulty sensor data, simply fixing the thermal management might not shift the average until the "learned" values are fully cleared and re-established over a complete drive cycle (cold start, warm up, highway driving).

It is also worth verifying the physical installation. If the new NGK sensor was not seated correctly in the manifold or if the ground wire connection was compromised during the swap, the ECU might be receiving erratic voltage spikes. This forces the fuel injection system to run rich constantly to prevent a lean misfire condition, which directly explains the drop from 8.3 k/l to 7.9 k/l.

If you have cleared adaptations and addressed the missing thermostat without seeing gains, the next logical step is to monitor the short-term and long-term fuel trim values via an OBD-II scanner. If these values are consistently positive (rich), the ECU is actively compensating for what it perceives as a lean condition caused by the new sensor's signal profile. In some legacy systems like the Mazda MPi engine found in your 323, swapping sensors without matching the exact factory calibration file can result in suboptimal performance that persists until the ECU fully adapts, which may take hundreds of kilometers rather than the immediate few hundred you have driven.
